sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: The song, which reportedly sold over three million copies,<ref name="Jackson5ABC">[http://www.jackson5abc.com/singles/ Sales statistics for Jackson 5 singles]. Retrieved March 17, 2008 {{Dead link|date=March 2026}}</ref> popularized the physically complicated [[Robot (dance)|robot]] dance technique, devised by Charles Washington in the late 1960s. [[Michael Jackson]] first performed the dance on television while singing "Dancing Machine" with the Jackson 5 on a Bob Hope special that aired September 26, 1973, but the cameraman cut away from Michael as he did the dance. A month later, on an episode of ''[[Soul Train]]'' on October 27, 1973 Michael again did the Robot dance and this time it was fully caught on camera.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-11-03 |title=Nov. 3, 1973: The Day 'The Robot' Dance Became Famous [EUR Video Throwback] |url=https://eurweb.com/nov-3-1973-the-day-the-robot-dance-became-famous-eur-video-throwback/ |access-date=2026-03-07 |website=EURweb}}</ref>  It was the group's first US top ten hit since 1971's "[[Sugar Daddy (The Jackson 5 song)|Sugar Daddy]]".  "Dancing Machine" brought the Jackson 5 their second [[Grammy Award]] nomination in [[Grammy Awards of 1975|1975]] for [[Grammy Award for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal|Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals]], losing to [[Rufus (band)|Rufus]] and [[Chaka Khan]]'s "[[Tell Me Something Good]]".
sections.text: The song, which reportedly sold over three million copies, popularized the physically complicated robot dance technique, devised by Charles Washington in the late 1960s. Michael Jackson first performed the dance on television while singing "Dancing Machine" with the Jackson 5 on a Bob Hope special that aired September 26, 1973, but the cameraman cut away from Michael as he did the dance. A month later, on an episode of Soul Train on October 27, 1973 Michael again did the Robot dance and this time it was fully caught on camera.  It was the group's first US top ten hit since 1971's "Sugar Daddy".  "Dancing Machine" brought the Jackson 5 their second Grammy Award nomination in 1975 for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals, losing to Rufus and Chaka Khan's "Tell Me Something Good".

sections.heading: Charts

In [[Canada]], "Dancing Machine" went to No. 2 on the [[RPM (magazine)|''RPM'' 100]]. In the United States, it hit No. 1 on ''[[Cash Box]]'' and reached No. 2 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], behind "[[The Streak (song)|The Streak]]" by [[Ray Stevens]].{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/1974-05-18|title=The Hot 100 Chart|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=2 January 2013}} In addition, it hit No. 1 on the [[R&B singles chart|R&B charts]].{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942–2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=287}} ''Billboard'' ranked it as the No. 5 song for 1974.[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1974]] {{col-begin}} {{col-2}} {|class="wikitable sortable" !Chart (1974) !Peak

sections.heading: Certifications and sales
Samples and cover versions
sections.wikitext:
"Dancing Machine" was most notably [[Sampling (music)|sampled]] by [[MC Hammer]], on his 1990 album ''[[Please Hammer Don't Hurt 'Em]]'', for "Dancin' Machine". It was also sampled again in 1990 by [[Vanilla Ice]] on the album ''[[To the Extreme]]'', later by [[Too Short|Too $hort]] (featuring [[Bun B]]) on the song "Shout It Out" and by [[Q-Tip (musician)|Q-Tip]] on the 2008 album ''[[The Renaissance (Q-Tip album)|The Renaissance]]'' for "Move". [[Yung Wun]] sampled it for "[[Tear It Up (Yung Wun song)|Tear It Up]]" on his album ''[[The Dirtiest Thirstiest]]'', in which the sample was uncredited and is taken directly from the film [[Drumline (film)|Drumline]], when the marching band performed it in medley.

Additionally, the song was [[cover version|covered]] by [[Roni Griffith]] in 1984. Another alternate [[remix]] version was released on ''[[The Original Soul of Michael Jackson]]'' in 1987. It was remixed with extra vocals and many overdubbed instruments, giving it an 80's pop feel rather than a mid 70's disco feel. [[Paula Abdul]] covered the song in 1997 as an unreleased demo. It was also covered by [[Suburban Legends]] on their [[Japan]]-only EP, ''[[Dance Like Nobody's Watching (EP)|Dance Like Nobody's Watching: Tokyo Nights]]''. A longer alternate version (4:25) appears on the ''[[I Want You Back! Unreleased Masters]]'' compilation released in 2009. A remix by [[Polow da Don]] was featured in a commercial for [[Svedka]]. This version was later released on the 2009 album ''[[The Remix Suite]]'', along with three other versions of the song, by [[Dave Audé]], [[Paul Oakenfold]] and [[Steve Aoki]]. In [[D-TV]], it was set to the ''[[Dance of the Hours]]'' segment from ''[[Fantasia (1940 film)|Fantasia]]''. [[Justin Timberlake]] interpolated part of the song (''watch her get down, watch her get down'') for the song "Murder" on his 2013 album ''[[The 20/20 Experience – 2 of 2]]''. The song was reworked and covered by English singer [[Laura Mvula]] in 2017, with the song produced by [[Naughty Boy]].
sections.text:
"Dancing Machine" was most notably sampled by MC Hammer, on his 1990 album Please Hammer Don't Hurt 'Em, for "Dancin' Machine". It was also sampled again in 1990 by Vanilla Ice on the album To the Extreme, later by Too $hort (featuring Bun B) on the song "Shout It Out" and by Q-Tip on the 2008 album The Renaissance for "Move". Yung Wun sampled it for "Tear It Up" on his album The Dirtiest Thirstiest, in which the sample was uncredited and is taken directly from the film Drumline, when the marching band performed it in medley.

Additionally, the song was covered by Roni Griffith in 1984. Another alternate remix version was released on The Original Soul of Michael Jackson in 1987. It was remixed with extra vocals and many overdubbed instruments, giving it an 80's pop feel rather than a mid 70's disco feel. Paula Abdul covered the song in 1997 as an unreleased demo. It was also covered by Suburban Legends on their Japan-only EP, Dance Like Nobody's Watching: Tokyo Nights. A longer alternate version (4:25) appears on the I Want You Back! Unreleased Masters compilation released in 2009. A remix by Polow da Don was featured in a commercial for Svedka. This version was later released on the 2009 album The Remix Suite, along with three other versions of the song, by Dave Audé, Paul Oakenfold and Steve Aoki. In D-TV, it was set to the Dance of the Hours segment from Fantasia. Justin Timberlake interpolated part of the song (watch her get down, watch her get down) for the song "Murder" on his 2013 album The 20/20 Experience – 2 of 2. The song was reworked and covered by English singer Laura Mvula in 2017, with the song produced by Naughty Boy.
